description: Glastonbury Festival from Pilton 1970 to the present — music, culture and British entertainment.
content_html:
The Origins of Glastonbury Festival

Glastonbury Festival began on a Somerset dairy farm. Worthy Farm, owned by dairy farmer Michael Eavis, hosted the first event on 19 September 1970, the day after Jimi Hendrix died. It was called the Pilton Pop, Folk and Blues Festival. Around 1,500 people attended and paid one pound, which included free milk from the farm. The event had a small makeshift stage; the atmosphere was informal, communal and countercultural.

The following year, in 1971, a larger event took place under the name Glastonbury Fayre. This event was influenced by the idealism of the late 1960s counterculture: free admission was charged, alternative therapies and crafts were offered alongside music, and the event was associated with hippie values and the idea of a natural, communal gathering. T. Rex (then billed as Tyrannosaurus Rex) had headlined the inaugural 1970 festival; David Bowie performed at the 1971 Glastonbury Fayre, giving an early morning performance that has passed into festival legend.

Key Fact

The first Glastonbury event took place on 19 September 1970, organised by Michael Eavis at Worthy Farm, Pilton, Somerset. Approximately 1,500 people attended and paid one pound each, including free milk. It was called the Pilton Pop, Folk and Blues Festival. The modern festival grew from this small, informal beginning.

The Pyramid Stage and Early Growth

The Pyramid Stage was first constructed in 1971 by Bill Harkin, a designer influenced by the alternative architecture movement. Built from scaffolding covered in a polythene skin and shaped as a pyramid — reportedly aligned with the Cheops pyramid — it gave the festival a striking visual identity that persisted through multiple rebuilds. The current Pyramid Stage is a large permanent steel structure, but its distinctive shape remains.

The festival did not run every year in its early decades. It was held intermittently in the early 1970s, and became an annual event from 1981. During the 1980s, the festival grew steadily in size and ambition. It gained a reputation not only for music but for its eclectic mix of theatre, circus, cabaret, healing fields and market stalls. It also developed a distinctive political character: the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) received a portion of the profits for many years from 1981.

The early 1990s exposed serious problems. The growth of the illegal rave and free party movement meant that Glastonbury became a magnet for large numbers of gatecrashers and festival-goers who had not paid. The 1992 festival saw estimated crowds of 70,000–80,000, far exceeding the licenced capacity, and there were significant public order concerns. Security became a serious issue throughout the mid-1990s.

The installation of the famous “Super Fence” — a steel perimeter fence several miles long — in 2002 transformed the festival’s physical form. The fence ended the tradition of free entry for those who could not afford a ticket or climbed in without paying. It made Glastonbury a secure, ticketed event with defined entrances. Critics argued it destroyed the festival’s countercultural spirit; supporters argued it saved the event from being shut down by the local council and police.

Glastonbury in the Twenty-First Century

By the 2000s, Glastonbury had established itself as the world’s largest greenfield music festival. Attendance regularly exceeded 200,000. The festival adopted a fallow year system — years with no festival — to allow the farmland to recover. Fallow years occurred in 1988, 1991, 1996, 2001 (foot-and-mouth disease), 2006, 2012, and 2018. The absence of a festival heightened demand and reinforced the event’s special character.

The programme diversified significantly. Dance music, which had been marginal in the early years, gained its own dedicated spaces in the 1990s and 2000s, including the Dance Village and the Park Stage. The “Legends Slot” — a Sunday afternoon performance by a veteran or legacy artist — became one of the most watched moments of each festival, featuring artists such as Shirley Bassey (2007), Paul McCartney (2004), and David Bowie (2000). The BBC began broadcasting extensive live footage from Glastonbury in the late 1990s, extending its audience far beyond the site itself.

Glastonbury connects to the broader themes of entertainment and leisure across the full period. It is a modern version of a tradition of communal, outdoor festivity that stretches back to medieval feast days and harvest festivals. Like the medieval fair, it combines music, performance, trade and community gathering in a rural setting. Like the Victorian music hall, it made entertainment accessible to large numbers of people — though now a ticket costs hundreds of pounds rather than a shilling.

The festival’s history also illustrates key themes of change: the shift from countercultural idealism (1970s free admission) to commercial spectacle (2000s sold-out ticketed event with corporate sponsorship); the impact of broadcasting technology (BBC coverage from the late 1990s turning a local Somerset event into a national cultural institution); and the tension between mass participation and exclusive access (the fencing controversy of 2002). It is a microcosm of how British popular entertainment changed over the twentieth century.

Key Fact

Glastonbury Festival links to the wider thematic study in two ways: it is a continuation of the tradition of communal outdoor festivity (medieval fairs, harvest festivals); and it shows the modern tension between accessible popular entertainment and commercial exclusivity. BBC coverage from the late 1990s and streaming from the 2010s transformed a local Somerset event into a global cultural institution.
exam_tip_html: The historic environment question requires you to link Glastonbury to the broader thematic narrative — not just to describe the festival in isolation. The 10% spec weighting reflects how important this connection is. A strong answer will use specific factual knowledge about Glastonbury (dates, key developments, the fencing controversy, BBC coverage) and then explicitly connect those facts to wider changes in British entertainment and leisure. For a 12-mark evaluation, you must also use your own contextual knowledge and reach a substantiated overall judgement — don’t just describe what the festival looked like at different times.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Glastonbury Festival began in 1970 at Worthy Farm, Pilton, with approximately 1,500 people paying one pound; it has grown into the world’s largest greenfield music festival with over 200,000 attendees.
  • Key turning points include: becoming annual from 1981; the Super Fence in 2002 ending free entry; BBC coverage from the late 1990s making it a national cultural institution; fallow years maintaining the farmland and demand.
  • Glastonbury links to the broader thematic study by continuing the tradition of communal outdoor festivity, illustrating the commercialisation of popular entertainment, and showing how broadcasting technology extended the reach of mass leisure beyond the physical site.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the first Glastonbury event held in 1970.
practice_questions.marks: One feature with detail: e.g. approximately 1,500 people attended and paid one pound, which included free milk from Worthy Farm / it was organised by Michael Eavis and was called the Pilton Pop, Folk and Blues Festival. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the development of Glastonbury Festival in the 1980s.
practice_questions.marks: Two features each developed: e.g. it became an annual event from 1981, growing in size and ambition (feature + detail); it developed a political character by donating a portion of profits to CND from 1981 (feature + detail). [4 marks: 2 per feature]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a security fence was built around Glastonbury Festival in 2002.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Developed explanation linking the 1990s rave movement, gatecrashing on a large scale (70,000–80,000 at the 1992 festival beyond licensed capacity), public order concerns, and the threat of closure by local council and police. Secure: Clear cause with supporting detail. Developing: Simple reason. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of BBC television coverage of Glastonbury Festival from the late 1990s.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Consequence developed, e.g. BBC coverage extended Glastonbury's audience from 200,000 on-site to millions watching at home, transforming a Somerset farm event into a national cultural institution; later streaming extended this globally. Secure: Clear consequence with supporting detail. Developing: Simple consequence. Emerging: Basic point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: How significant is Glastonbury Festival as evidence of changes in British popular entertainment since 1970?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses festival as evidence of change at the time (1970s countercultural origins, commercialisation by 2000s) AND over time (links to medieval communal festivity, Victorian music hall, mass broadcasting). Uses specific evidence. Secure: Clear analysis with examples. Developing: Some points. Emerging: Basic statement. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Glastonbury Festival shows that British popular entertainment has moved from communal and inclusive to commercial and exclusive since the 1970s.' How far do you agree with this view?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees with evidence of commercialisation (fencing 2002, ticket prices, corporate sponsorship). Challenges: BBC and streaming coverage made Glastonbury more accessible than ever to non-ticket holders; community values persist on site; charity donations. Reaches substantiated overall judgement. Secure: Both sides with evidence, overall judgement. Developing: Some argument, limited evidence. Emerging: Simple agree/disagree. [12 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Where does Glastonbury Festival take place, and who owns the site?
options: Glastonbury town centre, owned by Somerset County Council
Worthy Farm, Pilton, owned by Michael Eavis
A purpose-built arena in Bristol, leased from the local authority

knowledge_checks.q: When did Glastonbury Festival become an annual event?
The _____ Stage, first built in 1971 in a pyramid shape, is the main performance stage at Glastonbury Festival.
Glastonbury holds _____ years — years with no festival — to allow the farmland and the Eavis family to recover.
Match each year to its significance in Glastonbury's history:
right: First event at Worthy Farm — 1,500 people paying one pound
Super Fence built, ending free entry and gatecrashing
Festival became an annual event; CND began receiving a share of profits

flashcard_questions.q: When was the first Glastonbury event, and who organised it?
flashcard_questions.a: 19 September 1970, organised by Michael Eavis at Worthy Farm, Pilton.

flashcard_questions.q: How many people attended the first Glastonbury event, and how much did they pay?
flashcard_questions.a: Approximately 1,500 people, paying one pound each (including free milk).

flashcard_questions.q: What was the original name of the first Glastonbury event in 1970?
flashcard_questions.a: The Pilton Pop, Folk and Blues Festival — named after Pilton, the village where Worthy Farm is located.
The main performance stage at Glastonbury, first built in 1971 in a pyramid shape.

flashcard_questions.q: From what year did Glastonbury become an annual event?
What are fallow years at Glastonbury?
flashcard_questions.a: Years with no festival, to allow the farmland and the Eavis family to recover.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was the Super Fence built at Glastonbury in 2002?
flashcard_questions.a: To end gatecrashing and large-scale unauthorised entry that threatened the event's licence.

flashcard_questions.q: What political organisation received a share of Glastonbury's profits from 1981?
How does Glastonbury connect to the medieval tradition of communal festivity?
flashcard_questions.a: Like medieval fairs, it combines music, performance, trade and community gathering in a rural outdoor setting.

flashcard_questions.q: What effect did BBC television coverage from the late 1990s have on Glastonbury?
flashcard_questions.a: It extended the audience from 200,000 on-site to millions at home, making it a national cultural institution.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one notable artist from the early Glastonbury festivals (1970-1971).
flashcard_questions.a: T. Rex (then Tyrannosaurus Rex) headlined the 1970 festival; David Bowie performed an early morning set at the 1971 Glastonbury Fayre.

glossary_terms.definition: Michael Eavis's farm at Pilton in Somerset, the site of Glastonbury Festival from 1970 to the present day.
The main performance stage at Glastonbury Festival, built in 1971 in the shape of a pyramid, aligning approximately with the Egyptian pyramid of Cheops.
A policy at Glastonbury Festival of holding no event every five or six years to allow the land and the Eavis family to recover.
